beats.text: A program wants to print hello on the screen. But it runs in user mode, and the screen belongs to the kernel.
So it has to ask. That request is a system call: the program's door into the kernel.
Programs rarely knock on the door themselves. They call an A P I function, like printf in the C library, and the library makes the real system call. Here, write.
The library puts the system call number in a register, and runs a trap instruction.
The mode bit flips from one to zero. We are in kernel mode.
The kernel uses the number to find the right function in the system call table.
It does the work, and leaves the result in a register.
Then the bit flips back to one, and the program carries on in user mode.
Parameters travel in one of three ways: in registers, in a block of memory whose address sits in a register, or pushed onto the stack.
Every system call belongs to one of six families.
Process control, like fork and exit. File management, like open and read. Device management.
Information maintenance, like get time. Communications, like pipe. And protection, like chmod.
One design rule. Mechanism is how something is done. Policy is what will be done.
The timer is a mechanism. How long the timer is set for each user is a policy.
Keep them apart, and you can change the policy without rewriting the mechanism.
So how do you build the kernel itself?
A monolithic kernel puts everything into one big block. It is fast. But it is hard to maintain, and one bad driver can bring it all down.
A microkernel keeps only the minimum inside. Drivers and the file system run in user space, and talk by message passing.
A crash stays small, so it is reliable and secure. But every message costs time.
Linux takes a middle road: a modular kernel. A core, plus modules loaded when they are needed.
For the exam.
A system call is a controlled entry into the kernel.
Programs reach it through an A P I.
The mode bit flips twice.
Mechanism is how, policy is what.
Monolithic is fast, microkernel is safe.
